b: Habakkuk objects that God is ignoring evil, and then objects harder when told the remedy is Babylon. The exchange is preserved in full. It ends in one of the most defiant statements of trust in Scripture — though the crops fail and the stalls stand empty, yet I will rejoice.
The line 'the righteous will live by faith' comes from here, and Paul builds on it twice.

1.t: The book opens with a complaint against God, which is where a good many honest believers start.
Habakkuk's second complaint is harder than his first: the remedy looks worse than the disease.

2.h: The righteous shall live by his faith
2.t: Quoted three times in the New Testament and central to the Reformation.

3.h: Though the fig tree does not bud
3.t: The most defiant statement of trust in Scripture. Nothing has improved; the poet has simply decided where to stand.
